opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to understand it is to start from how diffusion works for images and then ask what the right analogue is for discrete data like text. In continuous diffusion, you take a clean image and gradually add Gaussian noise until it's pure static, and then you train a neural network to reverse that process step by step. For text, you can't really add Gaussian noise to a token in a meaningful way, so you need a different corruption process. And it turns out one of the simplest and most effective choices is masking: the "noise" is just replacing tokens with a special mask token.

So the forward process says: at noise level t, each token independently gets masked with some probability that increases with t. At the very end, everything is masked, and that's your equivalent of pure noise. The model is then trained to look at a partially masked sequence and predict what the original tokens were at the masked positions. At generation time, you start from a fully masked sequence and iteratively unmask, filling in tokens in parallel, refining over a number of steps.

What's nice is that, if you set things up correctly, this isn't just a heuristic. In our work on discrete diffusion, for example score entropy, we showed you can derive a principled training objective, essentially learning ratios of probabilities between sequences, the discrete analogue of the score function, and that gives you a proper bound on the likelihood. For the masking case, that objective simplifies to something that looks a lot like a weighted masked language modeling loss, like BERT, but with a specific weighting across masking rates that makes it a real generative model rather than just a representation learner.

It's also useful to contrast it with autoregressive models. An autoregressive model is in some sense a very specific masking schedule: you always unmask left to right, one token at a time. Masked diffusion relaxes that. The model learns to fill in any subset of tokens given any other subset, so at inference you can generate many tokens in parallel, do infilling, and trade compute for quality by choosing the number of steps. That's where a lot of the speed advantages come from, which is what we've been pushing on with commercial diffusion LLMs.

There are open questions, of course. Predicting many tokens at once independently can miss dependencies between them, so how you choose which tokens to unmask, and how many per step, matters a lot. But conceptually, I think of masking as the natural, simplest noise process for discrete data, and one that connects diffusion, masked language modeling, and autoregression in a single framework.

r001.rationale: It describes masking as the corruption process and says the model learns to recover original tokens from partially masked sequences.

r002.rationale: It contrasts left-to-right autoregression with predicting any subset from the remaining tokens, conveying that masked prediction can use context on both sides of a missing token.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I like to think about it is that diffusion, at its core, is about learning to reverse a corruption process. In the image world, the corruption is adding Gaussian noise. You take a clean image, you progressively add noise until it's basically pure static, and you train a model to undo that, step by step. At test time you start from noise and run the reverse process to generate a sample.

Now, for text, Gaussian noise doesn't make a lot of sense. Tokens are discrete, they're categorical variables. There's no notion of adding a little bit of noise to the word "cat" and getting something slightly different. So the question becomes: what's the right analog of noising for discrete data? And it turns out that masking is a very natural answer. Instead of adding noise, you corrupt the sequence by replacing some tokens with a special mask token. At the beginning of the forward process you have the clean sentence, and as you move forward you mask more and more tokens, until at the end everything is masked. That's your "pure noise" state.

The model is then trained to reverse that. You give it a partially masked sequence, and its job is to predict what the masked tokens should be. And if you squint, that looks a lot like BERT-style masked language modeling. The key difference is that in BERT you mask a fixed fraction, something like fifteen percent, and you're mostly using it as a representation learning objective. In a diffusion language model, you train across the whole range of masking rates, from almost nothing masked to almost everything masked, and you use the model as a generative process. You start from a fully masked sequence and iteratively unmask it. At each step the model fills in some tokens, you commit to some of those predictions, and you keep going until there are no masks left.

What's nice is that this gives you a principled training objective. You can show that the masked prediction loss, appropriately weighted across masking levels, is actually a bound on the log-likelihood of the data. So it's not just a heuristic; it's a proper likelihood-based generative model, in the same family as autoregressive models in that sense, just with a different factorization.

And the practical implications are what got us excited. Because you're predicting many tokens in parallel rather than one at a time, you're not fundamentally bound to generate left to right. You can get much better throughput, you can do infilling naturally, you can condition on arbitrary parts of the sequence, and you can trade off the number of denoising steps against quality. So masking is really the bridge that lets you take all the machinery from the diffusion literature and apply it to language in a way that's actually competitive at scale.

r001.rationale: It describes masking tokens as the text corruption process and says the model reverses it by predicting the masked tokens.

r002.rationale: It contrasts parallel, non-left-to-right generation with autoregressive generation and mentions infilling, but does not clearly say that predicting a missing token uses context from both sides.

astra-6.text:
One way to think about it is that you take a sentence and hide some of the tokens, and then you train a model to predict what was hidden from whatever context remains. That’s closely related to masked language modeling, like BERT. The key for diffusion is that you do this across different levels of corruption—from masking just a few tokens to masking essentially everything.

Then, to generate, you reverse that process. You start with a sequence of mask tokens, and the model gradually fills in the missing information. At first there’s very little context, so it has to make broad guesses. As more tokens become available, it can use those to make the remaining predictions more specific.

What’s interesting is that you’re not committed to generating strictly from left to right. You can use context on both sides of a missing word, and potentially predict many tokens in parallel. The challenge is making those predictions consistent with one another, which is why the iterative process matters.

r001.rationale: It says tokens are masked and the model is trained to predict what was hidden, then describes generation as reversing that corruption.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the model can use context on both sides of a missing word, unlike strictly left-to-right generation.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is that you take a piece of text and corrupt it by masking some of the tokens. Then you train a model to recover the original tokens from whatever is still visible. If you mask only a few tokens, that’s a relatively easy prediction problem. If you mask almost everything, the model has to learn much more about the overall structure of the text.

The diffusion perspective is to connect these different levels of corruption. You train across different masking rates, and then, at generation time, you start with a sequence of masks and gradually fill it in. Each step uses the context that’s available to predict more of the missing text.

So it’s closely related to masked language modeling. The key additional ingredient is learning a reverse process that you can run repeatedly to generate a complete sequence. And unlike left-to-right generation, you can predict multiple positions in parallel and use context on both sides.

r001.rationale: The response says text is corrupted by masking tokens, trains the model to recover them, and describes generation as repeatedly reversing that corruption.

r002.rationale: It contrasts left-to-right generation with predicting multiple positions in parallel using context on both sides.
